title: Tennessee Halts Execution After Two Lethal Injections; Governor Orders Review
summary:
Tennessee tried to carry out an execution on Wednesday night, but the attempt was stopped after two lethal injections. The state's governor has now ordered a review of how executions are done.

Christa Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. Both were teenagers in Knoxville at the time. The day was unusual even before the evening. The execution was scheduled for the morning, but a court order temporarily halted it. It took about nine hours to sort out, and then the U.S. Supreme Court gave officials the go-ahead.

At night, the state gave Pike two doses of the drug pentobarbital. Catherine Sweeney, a health reporter for WPLN in Nashville who was a media witness, and others described Pike as still talking after the first dose. After the second dose, she was heard breathing for more than 20 minutes. Much of this happened behind a closed curtain, and officials then moved the media witnesses out. They later confirmed that Pike was taken by ambulance to a medical facility. Officials have not said where she was taken.

The Tennessee Department of Correction says its team "followed every step in the protocol," and it is standing by the drug it uses. WPLN's news director, Tony Gonzalez, said the state's protocol does not consider what happens if a person is still alive after two doses. That is when the attempt was stopped.

Governor Bill Lee has ordered a third-party review. He also canceled the other execution that was scheduled for later this year in Tennessee. The governor says people are owed a legal, constitutional and effective method for carrying out the death penalty.

This is not the first time Tennessee has had trouble this year. In May, medical staff could not reach the veins of a man named Tony Carruthers, and the governor halted that execution. That led to bipartisan calls for a review, but the governor did not order one then. He later gave Carruthers a one-year reprieve. Earlier in his time as governor, Lee delayed executions for a couple of years after an investigation found that the state was not following its own protocol and had mishandled lethal drugs. It is unclear what will happen next for Pike, and Gonzalez said it is unclear whether she would receive a reprieve like the one Carruthers received.
why_it_matters: The story shows how a state responds when a serious process does not go as planned, and why officials are asked to review their own rules. It also shows why reporters and witnesses matter when the public wants to know what happened.

options: The governor visited the prison in person
Reporters were not allowed into the building
A court order temporarily halted the morning execution
The state changed the drug it planned to use

options: About nine days

options: It says the governor must watch the execution
It requires three doses of the drug in every case
It does not consider what happens if a person is still alive after two doses
It lets reporters decide when to stop

options: A court canceled his sentence for good

options: He gave him a one-year reprieve
He ordered a new trial
He gave him a full pardon
He moved him to another state

questions.question: What did an investigation find earlier in Lee's time as governor?
options: The state was not following its own protocol and had mishandled lethal drugs

background_read: Christa Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, when both were teenagers in Knoxville.
Lethal injection is the method Tennessee uses for executions, and the state follows a written protocol for it.

A third-party review is done by people from outside the department, so that the findings do not come only from the officials being checked.
